request:
Hi, I'm in HL Bio and we've been set an "evaluate the evidence" homework on industrial melanism in the peppered moth. My teacher keeps saying the textbook version is "too tidy" and that we have to show who actually found what, when, and which bits got challenged later. I don't want you to write it for me, I need to understand it well enough to write my own, so could you explain:

(a) the actual sequence of evidence: when the dark form first turned up, who proposed bird predation and camouflage as the cause, what Kettlewell did (where, when, and roughly what his recapture numbers showed) and what happened to the dark form after the Clean Air Act. Please attribute each claim to a person or paper and a year, and say how confident you are in each number rather than just stating it.

(b) the criticisms of Kettlewell's experiments in the 1990s and 2000s and how they were answered. Which criticisms were fair and which weren't? I've seen a claim online that the whole thing was faked and I need to know whether biologists take that seriously.

(c) a calculation [4 marks]. These numbers are from our class sheet and are made up for the exercise: a wood near an industrial city, 1960 sample: 450 moths, 405 melanic and 45 pale (typica). Same wood in 2000: 320 moths, 64 melanic and 256 pale. The melanic form (carbonaria) is dominant at a single locus. Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to estimate the frequency of the carbonaria allele in each year, and the proportion of the melanic moths in 1960 that were heterozygous. Then explain why the allele frequency and the phenotype frequency don't fall by the same amount. Show every step and state the assumptions you're making.

(d) what the modern genetics says the mutation actually is and roughly when it happened. Is that agreed or still argued?

Also, is it OK to call this "evolution" or do I have to say "natural selection changed the allele frequency"? My teacher is picky about wording.
strong_answer_must: Not write the student's homework; explain the evidence, the reasoning and the calculation so the student can write it, optionally suggesting a structure.

(a) Give an attributed timeline with years and hedged figures: the first recorded melanic (carbonaria) specimen is usually dated 1848 in Manchester (a commonly cited record, not a measured origin); by the end of the 1890s melanic moths made up the large majority (figures of about 95-98 per cent are often quoted for Manchester) of some industrial populations; J. W. Tutt (1896) proposed that birds eat the form that is worse camouflaged, with soot-darkened and lichen-free surfaces favouring the dark form; J. B. S. Haldane (1924) used the speed of the rise to estimate that carbonaria needed a selective advantage of roughly 50 per cent per generation (a model-based estimate that depends on assumptions about generation time and starting frequency); H. B. D. Kettlewell carried out mark-release-recapture experiments in a polluted wood near Birmingham (1953, repeated 1955) and an unpolluted wood in Dorset (1955), finding that the better-camouflaged form was recaptured roughly twice as often as the other (figures in the region of 27 per cent versus 13 per cent in Birmingham, and the reverse ranking in Dorset), with bird predation filmed and observed directly (Niko Tinbergen); results published in Heredity in 1955 and 1956. Say the recapture percentages are recalled approximately and that the student should check them against the original papers or their textbook before quoting them.

(a) State what happened after pollution controls: the UK Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 reduced soot and sulfur dioxide; long-term monitoring documented the decline of carbonaria, including Clarke, Mani and Wynne (1985) at Caldy Common on the Wirral (carbonaria above 90 per cent around 1959, falling steadily afterwards), Grant, Owen and Clarke (1996) showing a parallel rise and fall in Britain and the north-eastern United States, and later surveys summarised by Cook (2003) and Cook and Saccheri (2013) showing carbonaria at a few per cent at Caldy Common by the 2000s. Exact percentages must be hedged as approximate.

(a) Explain the mechanism in Biology terms: variation (heritable melanic allele), differential survival through visual predation by birds, change in allele frequency over generations (one generation per year in Britain); the environment changed the direction of selection, not the moths.

(b) Identify the real criticisms with attribution: moths rest mainly on the underside of branches and in the canopy rather than on exposed trunks (Mikkola 1979 and 1984; Howlett and Majerus 1987); Kettlewell released lab-reared moths in daylight at unnaturally high densities, which could inflate predation; photographs of dead moths pinned to trunks were illustrations, not the experiment; the recovery of lichens lagged behind the decline of carbonaria, so lichen cover alone does not explain the reversal (noted by Grant and co-workers); migration between polluted and unpolluted areas complicates allele-frequency comparisons. Sargent, Millar and Lambert (1998) proposed alternative explanations; Jerry Coyne's 1998 review in Nature of Majerus's book 'Melanism: Evolution in Action' (1998) suggested the example should be dropped, which Majerus and others argued went far beyond what the criticisms justified.

(b) Address the fraud claim correctly: Judith Hooper's 2002 book 'Of Moths and Men' insinuated that Kettlewell's data were manipulated; this is not accepted by biologists and has been rebutted in detail (for example David Rudge's 2005 analysis of the fraud allegation and reviews by Bruce Grant and by Michael Majerus); the fair criticisms concern experimental design and realism, not honesty.

(b) Describe how the criticisms were answered: Michael Majerus ran a six-year predation experiment (2001-2007) in a Cambridge garden, releasing nearly five thousand moths at natural densities and natural resting positions, and found that carbonaria suffered significantly higher predation in an unpolluted environment, with the result presented in 2007 and published posthumously by Cook, Grant, Saccheri and Mallet (Biology Letters, 2012); together with the documented decline after pollution controls, this is widely regarded as confirming bird predation as the main selective agent. Say that the relative contribution of other factors (non-visual selection, migration) remains discussed, but the core case is well supported.

(c) Correct Hardy-Weinberg working with assumptions stated: let p = frequency of the dominant carbonaria allele and q = frequency of the recessive typica allele, p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1. Because typica is recessive, pale moths are homozygous recessive, so q^2 = frequency of pale moths. 1960: q^2 = 45/450 = 0.100, so q = 0.316 (0.3162) and p = 0.684 (0.6838). 2000: q^2 = 256/320 = 0.800, so q = 0.894 (0.8944) and p = 0.106 (0.1056). The carbonaria allele frequency falls from about 0.68 to about 0.11. Must take the square root of the pale-moth frequency, not of the melanic frequency.

(c) Proportion of melanic moths heterozygous in 1960: 2pq = 2 x 0.6838 x 0.3162 = 0.432 (0.4325); p^2 = 0.468 (0.4675); melanic total = 0.900; heterozygous share = 0.4325/0.900 = 0.48, so about 48 per cent of the 1960 melanic moths were heterozygous (equivalently 2pq/(1 - q^2)). Optional extension: in 2000, 2pq = 0.189 and p^2 = 0.011, so about 94 per cent of the remaining melanic moths were heterozygous.

(c) Explain the mismatch: the phenotype frequency of melanic moths is p^2 + 2pq = 1 - q^2, not p, because heterozygotes look melanic; with dominance, a small pale fraction (0.10) still corresponds to a sizeable typica allele frequency (0.32), and most of the melanic allele's decline is hidden inside heterozygotes; in this exercise the allele frequency fell by about 0.58 (from 0.68 to 0.11, a relative fall of roughly 85 per cent) while the melanic phenotype fell by 0.70 (from 0.90 to 0.20, a relative fall of roughly 78 per cent), so the two do not move together. Note that selection against a dominant allele is effective at low frequency because every carrier is exposed to predation, whereas a recessive allele hides in heterozygotes.

(c) State the assumptions and limits: the Hardy-Weinberg equation assumes a large randomly mating population with no selection, migration or mutation, which is exactly what is not true here, so it is being used only as an estimation tool on the assumption that genotype frequencies among newly emerged adults are in Hardy-Weinberg proportions before selection acts; single locus with complete dominance and two alleles (ignoring the intermediate insularia alleles); the sample is a sample, so the estimate carries sampling error. Report the unrounded value before the rounded value and give rounding to 2 or 3 significant figures to match the data.

(c) Any mark awarded must appear with the word 'provisional' in the same sentence and be tied to specific steps (identifying q^2 from the recessive phenotype, correct square roots, heterozygote proportion, correct explanation of dominance).

(d) Modern genetics, attributed and hedged: van't Hof and co-workers (Science, 2011) mapped the carbonaria locus to one region of chromosome 17; van't Hof and co-workers (Nature, 2016) identified the causal mutation as a large transposable element insertion (about 22 kb) in an intron of the cortex gene, and estimated from the pattern of linked variation that the mutation arose around 1819 (with an uncertainty range of a few decades), consistent with a first record in 1848 after some spread; the same genomic region is involved in wing-pattern variation in Heliconius butterflies (Nadeau and co-workers, 2016). Say that the identity of the insertion is well supported, that the exact developmental mechanism by which it darkens the wing is still being investigated, and that the 1819 date is a model-based estimate, not a record.

Answer the wording question: evolution is a change in the heritable characteristics (allele frequencies) of a population over generations; natural selection is one mechanism that causes it. The peppered moth case is evolution by natural selection within a species (a change in allele frequency, not the origin of a new species), so both phrasings are correct provided the student says what changed (allele frequency in the population) and what caused it (differential predation); avoid saying individual moths adapted or changed colour.

Keep the explanation at the Biology level (selection, allele frequency, camouflage, predation) without adopting an ESS or Geography framing, and not invent additional studies, percentages or quotations.

End with a single 'Sources:' line in the gate format (here 'Sources: none consulted (no retrieval in this session)' unless course notes are described in general words), with no URLs and no internal codes.
pitfalls: Writing the homework for the student instead of explaining.
Lamarckian or individual-level phrasing: moths 'turned dark to match the trees', 'adapted to pollution', or 'evolved during their lifetime'.

Mis-attribution or mis-dating: Kettlewell's experiments placed in the 1920s or 1960s; bird predation hypothesis credited to Kettlewell or Darwin rather than Tutt (1896); Haldane's estimate omitted or stated as a measured value; the Clean Air Act given as 1952 or the 1970s; Majerus's experiment attributed to Kettlewell or dated to the 1990s; the 2012 publication credited to Majerus alone.
Stating recapture percentages, 1890s melanic percentages, the 1819 origin date or the Caldy Common figures with false precision and no hedging, or inventing numbers.
Treating Hooper's fraud allegation as accepted, or at the other extreme claiming there were no legitimate criticisms of Kettlewell's design.
Saying the carbonaria decline proves lichens recovered first, or that soot alone explains everything, without noting the lichen-timing issue.

Calculation errors: taking the square root of the melanic frequency (0.90) to get p; using the melanic frequency directly as p; forgetting that heterozygotes are melanic; reporting 2pq as the proportion of melanic moths heterozygous without dividing by the melanic total; arithmetic slips (q for 1960 is 0.316, not 0.1 or 0.05); rounding before the final step; giving no units or no significant-figure justification.
Claiming the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, or failing to flag that using the equation in a population under selection is an approximation with stated assumptions.

Saying allele frequency and phenotype frequency fall by the same amount, or explaining the mismatch by anything other than dominance and the square relationship (for example invoking mutation or random drift as the reason).

Getting the genetics wrong: naming a different gene, calling the mutation a point mutation or a deletion, dating the mutation to 1848 (that is the first record, not the origin), or presenting the 1819 estimate as certain.
Saying the peppered moth case is 'not really evolution' because no new species formed, or conversely calling it speciation.

Fabricated paper titles, journals, page numbers or URLs; a missing or malformed Sources line; awarding marks for (c) without the word 'provisional'; leaking any internal code or knowledge-document name.
